column1: What is an ordinary, nonindexed SQL Server view?
column2: A virtual table defined by a SELECT query.
column3: It retrieves data from underlying objects rather than storing a separate result set.

column1: Which statement creates dbo.vProducts from ProductID and Name in dbo.Products?
column2: CREATE VIEW dbo.vProducts AS SELECT ProductID, Name FROM dbo.Products;
column3: Callers can query the view in a FROM clause.

column1: Why list view columns explicitly instead of using SELECT *?
column2: To keep the exposed columns deliberate and stable as tables change.
column3: Explicit columns prevent accidental dependence on every column of the base table.

column1: Which view clause requires inserted or updated rows to remain visible through the view?
column2: WITH CHECK OPTION.
column3: A modification through the view fails when the resulting row violates its filter.

column1: What permission pattern lets a view expose selected columns without granting direct access to its base table?
column2: Grant SELECT on the view while restricting direct table access.
column3: Review other access paths because the view alone does not remove existing permissions.

column1: Which type of SQL Server view physically stores its result set?
column2: An indexed view.
column3: Unlike an ordinary view, it maintains indexed data when its underlying data changes.

column1: Why avoid deeply nested views?
column2: They make query logic harder to understand, maintain, and optimize.
column3: Keep each view focused instead of hiding many layers of dependencies.

column1: Which programmability object fits explicitly called, multi-step data modifications with transaction control?
column2: A stored procedure.
column3: It can coordinate changes across multiple tables in one transaction.

column1: Which T-SQL statement calls dbo.GetCustomerOrders with CustomerID 42?
column2: EXEC dbo.GetCustomerOrders @CustomerID = 42;
column3: Named arguments identify which parameter receives each value.

column1: Which statement defines dbo.GetOrders with an integer @CustomerID parameter?
column2: CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetOrders @CustomerID INT AS SELECT OrderID FROM dbo.Orders WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID;
column3: Procedure parameters start with @ and include a data type.

column1: How does a stored procedure make an input parameter optional?
column2: Declare a default value for that parameter.
column3: For example, @StartDate DATE = NULL permits a call that omits @StartDate.

column1: Which keyword marks a procedure parameter that can return a value to the caller?
column2: OUTPUT.
column3: For example, declare @Total DECIMAL(10,2) OUTPUT in the procedure definition.

column1: What does SET NOCOUNT ON suppress in a stored procedure?
column2: Messages reporting the number of rows affected by statements.
column3: It reduces unnecessary messages without suppressing SELECT result sets.

column1: What cached SQL Server structure can reduce repeated procedure compilation work?
column2: An execution plan.
column3: A cached plan can be reused, but recompilation and cache eviction remain possible.

column1: When must a stored procedure validate input parameters?
column2: Before it performs work that depends on those parameters.
column3: Reject invalid input explicitly rather than processing bad data.

column1: What naming form identifies an object's schema explicitly in T-SQL?
column2: schema.object, such as dbo.Orders.
column3: Schema-qualified names avoid ambiguity about the intended object.

column1: Which prefix must user-defined SQL Server procedure names avoid because it denotes system procedures?
column2: sp_.
column3: Use a descriptive name such as dbo.GetCustomerOrders instead.

column1: Which T-SQL construct routes catchable execution errors to an error-handling block?
column2: TRY...CATCH.
column3: Put the main operation in TRY and the error response in CATCH.

column1: Which function returns the caught error's message inside a CATCH block?
column2: ERROR_MESSAGE().
column3: Use the message when recording or reporting the failure.

column1: Which system variable counts active transaction nesting before a procedure's CATCH block attempts a rollback?
column2: @@TRANCOUNT.
column3: A positive value indicates an active transaction, not that it is committable.

column1: Which function type returns one calculated value for use in a SQL expression?
column2: A scalar user-defined function.
column3: Use it for reusable calculations such as tax or formatted text.

column1: Which scalar function clause declares the result's data type?
column2: RETURNS followed by the data type.
column3: For example, RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2) defines a decimal result.

column1: What makes a calculation deterministic?
column2: It returns the same result for the same inputs.
column3: A deterministic calculation does not depend on the changing current time.

column1: Why does GETDATE() make the module's tenure function nondeterministic?
column2: Its result depends on the current system time.
column3: The same hire-date argument can produce a different result on another date.

column1: How can a date-based calculation avoid reading GETDATE() inside its function body?
column2: Accept an as-of date as an input parameter.
column3: Explicit dates make the time dependency visible to callers.

column1: What database side effect is prohibited inside a T-SQL user-defined function?
column2: Modifying persistent database state.
column3: A function cannot insert business rows into a permanent table.

column1: Why can a noninlined scalar function slow a query over many rows?
column2: Repeated function calls add per-row execution overhead.
column3: Inlining or rewriting the calculation can avoid some of this overhead.

column1: Which statement changes an existing scalar function without dropping and recreating it?
column2: ALTER FUNCTION.
column3: Altering the existing object preserves its granted permissions.

column1: Which catalog view helps identify SQL expression dependencies before dropping a function?
column2: sys.sql_expression_dependencies.
column3: Review dependencies before removing a function used by other database objects.

column1: Which statement removes dbo.CalculateSalesTax only if it exists?
column2: DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS dbo.CalculateSalesTax;
column3: IF EXISTS avoids a missing-object error, but does not remove dependency restrictions.

column1: Which object returns a parameterized result set that a query can use as a table source?
column2: A table-valued function.
column3: Unlike a stored procedure, its result can participate directly in FROM and JOIN operations.

column1: What defines the result of an inline table-valued function?
column2: A single SELECT query after RETURN.
column3: The function does not build its result through a procedural statement block.

column1: What stores the returned rows inside a multi-statement table-valued function?
column2: A named table variable declared in its RETURNS clause.
column3: The function body populates that variable before returning.

column1: How does the optimizer integrate an inline table-valued function into a calling query?
column2: It expands the function's query into the calling query.
column3: This exposes the relational logic for optimization rather than treating it as a separate procedural result.

column1: Which operator passes each left-side CustomerID into a TVF and excludes customers with no returned rows?
column2: CROSS APPLY.
column3: For example, use CROSS APPLY dbo.GetCustomerOrders(c.CustomerID) AS o.

column1: Which trigger category responds automatically to INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statements?
column2: A DML trigger, for data manipulation events.
column3: It attaches to a table or, for INSTEAD OF behavior, a view.

column1: Which trigger category responds to schema events such as CREATE TABLE or DROP TABLE?
column2: A DDL trigger, for data definition events.
column3: Use it to audit or control applicable schema changes.

column1: When does a SQL Server AFTER DML trigger run?
column2: After the triggering operation and its constraint checks succeed, before transaction commit.
column3: AFTER does not mean that the transaction is already committed.

column1: Which trigger type replaces the requested data modification with custom logic?
column2: INSTEAD OF.
column3: It can implement modifications through a view that is not directly updatable.

column1: Which DML trigger logical table contains new row values after INSERT or UPDATE?
column2: inserted.
column3: An UPDATE exposes new values in inserted and old values in deleted.

column1: Which DML trigger logical table contains old row values from DELETE or UPDATE?
column2: deleted.
column3: For a DELETE, it contains the removed rows.

column1: What does UPDATE(Price) detect inside a DML trigger?
column2: An attempted INSERT or UPDATE affecting Price, not necessarily a changed value.
column3: It can return TRUE even when an UPDATE assigns the existing value.

column1: Why must a SQL Server DML trigger handle multiple rows?
column2: One triggering statement can affect many rows in a single trigger invocation.
column3: Do not assume that inserted or deleted contains just one row.

column1: Which coding approach lets a trigger process every affected row without a cursor?
column2: Set-based operations over inserted and deleted.
column3: Use joins and grouped aggregates when several affected rows share a parent key.

column1: How can a trigger defer expensive work without performing it in the current transaction?
column2: Record work in a queue for separate asynchronous processing.
column3: Keep the trigger's own transactional work short and focused.
